item.title: Why 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awards optogenetics
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
The larger impact of optogenetics may lie in what it allows scientists to ask. By turning carefully selected nerve cells on or off, researchers can continue to unravel one of humanity's greatest mysteries: how the brain works. STOCKHOLM, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institutet awarded the prize for optogenetics and described it as a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the living brain. WHO ARE THE LAUREATES? Karl Deisseroth is a U.S.-born professor at Stanford University and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, both born in Germany, are professors at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Wuerzburg, respectively. "Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the institute said in a press release. The laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.19 million U.S. dollars). WHAT IS OPTOGENETICS? Optogenetics refers to a method for controlling nerve signals with light. The story began with a simple question: how can a single-celled green alga swim toward light even though it has no brain? Peter Hegemann studied Chlamydomonas, an alga that can detect light and rapidly change its movement. He suspected that its light sensor might also act as an ion channel. Working with Georg Nagel, Hegemann identified proteins known as channelrhodopsins. When exposed to blue light, these proteins open a channel through the cell membrane. Charged ions then flow into the cell, producing an electrical response. Crucially, when researchers introduced the genes encoding these proteins into other cells, those cells also became sensitive to light. Karl Deisseroth introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats. In 2005, his team showed that flashes of blue light could trigger nerve signals with millisecond precision. Two years later, the approach was successfully used in the brains of living mice. The method became known as optogenetics and gained global impact. WHY DID THIS CHANGE NEUROSCIENCE? The adult human brain contains around 90 billion nerve cells, or neurons, each forming thousands of connections with other cells. Neural pathways can stretch across distant parts of the brain, while neurons controlling very different functions may be packed closely together. For decades, scientists could observe which parts of the brain became active when an animal moved, formed a memory or experienced an emotion. Such observations could show that brain activity and behavior were linked without revealing whether one directly caused the other. Optogenetics changed that by allowing scientists to activate selected neurons and observe what happened next, making it possible to test cause and effect with far greater precision. Researchers have identified neural circuits involved in pain, social behavior, thirst, feeding, reward and attention. They have also pinpointed neurons that help regulate functions ranging from the body clock to fever responses triggered by the immune system. "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of," said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. COULD IT HELP TREAT DISEASE? For now, optogenetics remains primarily a research tool, helping scientists investigate how brain circuits malfunction in conditions including depression, anxiety, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Anna Wedell, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, said that researchers can first identify cells involved in conditions such as dementia and addiction in animal models, and then use imaging and other methods to explore how those findings may apply to humans. Clinical research has also begun. Qiang Pan Hammarstrom, a member of the Nobel Committee and professor of Clinical Immunology at Karolinska Institutet, told Xinhua that optogenetics has already shown clinical potential in retinitis pigmentosa, a rare genetic eye disease, where light-sensitive proteins can be used to stimulate surviving retinal cells and partially restore vision. The larger impact of optogenetics may lie in what it allows scientists to ask. By turning carefully selected nerve cells on or off, researchers can continue to unravel one of humanity's greatest mysteries: how the brain works.■

item.title: Ancient temple draws visitors as cultural tourism booms in Shanxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
TAIYUAN, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- For years, Yang Liangen saw strangers as a threat. After a series of break-in attempts at a 900-year-old temple in north China's Shanxi Province, Yang moved into the compound in 1997, sleeping behind its gates and guarding its rare sculptures and wooden structures. Nearly three decades later, he eagerly waits for strangers to arrive. "We used to be afraid when people came," Yang said. "Now we hope they will come." Located in Xiaonan Village in Jincheng City, Erxian Temple fully opened to the public in 2024 as interest in Shanxi's ancient architecture surged following the release of "Black Myth: Wukong," a blockbuster Chinese video game. During China's National Day holiday that year, Yang counted 1,280 visitors in a single day -- a record for a site whose gates had long been kept mostly shut. The crowds have continued to grow, with more than 4,300 people visiting the temple from Oct. 1 to 3 this year. The change at Erxian Temple reflects a broader shift across China, as growing interest in cultural tourism brings new attention to historic buildings that for decades were little known beyond their local communities. Built in 1097, Erxian Temple is a major national cultural heritage site. Its main hall is known for rare Song Dynasty (960-1279) painted sculptures and an exceptionally well-preserved miniature wooden architectural structure known locally as the "sky bridge." Dubbed China's "above-ground cultural relics museum," Shanxi is home to over 28,000 ancient structures. The province also preserves more than 12,000 painted sculptures and 24,000 square meters of murals from the Tang Dynasty (618-907) onward. PRESERVED BEHIND THE GATES For Yang, the new attention marks a dramatic change from the late 1990s. Facing growing risks to the temple in 1997, Yang, then the village Party secretary, took responsibility for Erxian Temple and moved in with his wife. The couple kept watch day and night. On one occasion, Yang's wife rushed outside with a flashlight after two people were spotted apparently chiseling through a wall, sending them fleeing. No theft has occurred since Yang became its caretaker. A major restoration completed in 2014 repaired the compound and revived its two-courtyard layout. Surveillance cameras were installed, giving the couple what Yang described as their first truly restful sleep in years. But the gates largely remained closed. Visits by preservation experts became important opportunities for Yang. He followed them around, learning about Song Dynasty construction and the temple's rare architectural features. As architecture enthusiasts began making their way to the village, Yang sometimes made exceptions to let them inside and shared what he had learned. "They had come such a long way," Yang said. "Maybe they would only come once in their lives. How could I not let them see it?" Over time, Yang turned himself from a guard into an unofficial guide. FINDING NEW AUDIENCES Years of restoration and improved security eventually made it possible for more people to see what Yang had spent decades protecting. In late 2022, an upgrade of Erxian Temple's security system was launched. Around the same time, local heritage enthusiasts formed a volunteer association in Jincheng City to support heritage site caretakers, organize educational visits and train volunteer guides. In August 2024, Jincheng began opening 18 nationally and provincially protected heritage sites to the public on Sundays on a trial basis before fully opening them in October. Erxian Temple was included. "The temple didn't become popular overnight," said Zhang Jianjun, one of the association's founders. "Without all those years of preparation, we wouldn't have been ready when the crowds came." The association now has more than 400 members, including Zhang Jie, a local charter driver who first visited Erxian Temple while taking customers around Shanxi in 2024. Standing among centuries-old sculptures and elaborate woodwork, he realized how little he knew about the heritage of his own home province. "I felt ashamed, but also curious," he said. He began studying traditional architecture, joined the volunteer association and now shares what he has learned with tourists. At the Hanging Temple in Datong City, Chen Ruiyan recalled a recent road trip she and her husband had taken from Guangdong Province to Shanxi, visiting more than a dozen historic sites across the province. Inspired by films and animations featuring Shanxi's ancient architecture, they had studied traditional architectural features before setting out. "Beyond their aesthetic impact, ancient wooden buildings have a sense of quietness and vitality," Chen said. Beyond Shanxi, efforts to preserve historic architecture are also bringing old buildings closer to contemporary life. In Fujian Province, traditional Tulou, or earthen buildings, are being preserved and given new uses, while in Guizhou Province, more than 12,000 endangered traditional buildings have undergone emergency restoration. China's latest five-year plan for cultural heritage calls for stronger systematic protection while making preservation efforts more accessible and beneficial to the public. Wang Chunbo, a researcher specializing in ancient architecture, sculptures and murals in Shanxi, said the growing interest in historic architecture reflects a deeper engagement with traditional culture among younger Chinese. "Young people are no longer satisfied with simply checking a destination off their list," Wang said. "Historic buildings are becoming cultural spaces they can experience, engage with and share." Li Junda, a university student studying anthropology in London, traveled to Shanxi after encountering Yang's story online. What struck him was how the temple's history was still carried by the people around it. "At the British Museum, I saw many Chinese artifacts on display, identified simply by their dynasties," Li said. "Here in Shanxi, the heritage is still 'alive,' because villagers like Yang are here to tell the stories behind it." ■

item.title: A Chinese county's violins go global
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- A knife turns gently against a scroll taking shape in a workshop. The craftsman blows softly, sending fine shavings dancing in a ray of sunlight, and the air is filled with the scent of spruce and maple. The scene could easily belong in Cremona, Italy. Yet it is unfolding in Queshan, a county of about 374,500 people in central China's Henan Province that has quietly become one of the world's major sources of handmade violins. The craft originated in 16th-century Italy and spread across the globe by the 18th century. In the 1980s, villagers from Queshan joined the tide of migrant workers heading to faraway cities. Many found jobs in violin factories in Beijing. Over the years, they built a reputation as master craftsmen. Some even ran their own workshops. In 2015, Queshan began calling its natives home and laid plans for a violin industrial park. More than 60 luthiers returned to start businesses, assigning production roles to households where villagers can be trained and employed. Unlike factory workers on city assembly lines, Queshan's craftsmen often specialize in a single stage, sawing timber, carving plates, fitting bodies, or cutting scrolls. They can also take components home and set their own hours. He Ruixia is one of those returnees. "My hours are flexible, and I'm paid for each piece I finish," she said, bending over a violin while her husband assembled a cello nearby. "Since I came back, I earn more and I'm happier," she said. "It's easier to look after my family and still get my work done." The instruments she makes will be shipped from the northern port of Tianjin to the United States, the biggest overseas market for Queshan violins by both volume and value. Queshan holds more than 80 percent of the domestic market for mid to high-end handmade violins, according to Jiang Baolin, secretary-general of the Queshan Handmade Violin Makers Association. Taking advantage of the digital age, local workshops are now reaching buyers through social media. In a livestream at a factory in Zhugou Township, a host works with a musician testing instruments live as customers from Australia, Russia and France place orders online. "Cross-border e-commerce presents our violins to customers across the globe," Jiang said. "Short videos and livestreaming enable overseas customers to see for themselves the quality of Chinese violin-making. People in the trade have long known that good handmade violins come from Queshan, but there was no channel to buy them before." Today, violins made in Queshan are sold in more than 30 countries and regions, including the United States, Italy, France and Germany. The county has built a complete industrial chain spanning timber processing, accessory carving and spray-painting. Its 144 violin-making and supporting businesses employ more than 2,600 local people, who turn out about 400,000 violins a year, generating an annual industrial output of 600 million yuan (89.5 million U.S. dollars). The industry has also been a path out of poverty. In February 2020, Queshan was among the last 14 impoverished counties in Henan Province to be removed from China's poverty list. The violin continues to inspire the next generation. According to Jiang, several primary schools in the county offer violin classes, giving children a chance to learn the instrument their own families make. "Several young people are now studying at conservatories in Beijing, Tianjin, Xi'an and Shanghai," he said. ■

item.title: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
* Chinese travelers have ventured farther during the National Day holiday, with family trips and experience-oriented travel on the rise. * Former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. * More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different. Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies. "It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China. LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings. Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes. "The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said. Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars). The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences. Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products. As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services. During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3. RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year. The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns. At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting. On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them. China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference. Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees. With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers. Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls. Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said. On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year. "More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu. CHINA HAUL While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs. Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand. Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere." China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration. That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry. (Video reporters: Chen Si, Lin Long, Ji Zijian, Sun Qing and Zhong Chao; Video editors: Zhang Mocheng and Hong Ling) ■

item.title: World Insights: What could shape Brazil's tight presidential runoff
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
by Xinhua writers Lu Junyu, Chen Haoquan and Wu Hao RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential election is heading to a runoff on Oct. 25 after a tight first-round vote on Sunday, with Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party and incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party separated by only about 2 percentage points. The first-round results underscored the continued polarization of Brazilian politics, with the two candidates together securing over 90 percent of valid votes. Over the next three weeks, attention will focus on why the race remains so close, how U.S.-Brazil ties could affect the campaign, and where the two candidates could find additional support. WHY THE CLOSE RACE? The first-round vote was highly concentrated around the two leading candidates. Flavio Bolsonaro led the first round with about 47 percent of valid votes, followed by Lula with about 45 percent, while all other candidates received less than 5 percent each. Brazilian media said the gap of less than 2 percentage points between the two was the narrowest presidential first-round margin since Brazil's return to democracy. Both candidates also have relatively firm political bases but face considerable public rejection; therefore, the runoff begins with two relatively consolidated political camps, leaving less room to win over committed supporters of the other side, local media reported, citing political analysts. Under Brazil's electoral rules, voters can decline to support any candidate by casting blank or null ballots, a choice that can also serve as an expression of political discontent. Low voter enthusiasm has added another layer of uncertainty to the election. According to official results, with more than 99 percent of ballots counted, turnout in the first round was weighed down by an abstention rate of 21.08 percent, while blank and null ballots together accounted for about 5 percent of votes cast. A pre-election survey by Brazilian pollster Datafolha found that 47 percent of respondents were less interested in this election than in the previous one. Another poll, by consultancy Quaest, showed that 23 percent were "completely uninterested" in the race, while a further 10 percent said they might abstain or cast a blank or null ballot. With the two political camps already highly consolidated, supporters of the eliminated candidates and voters aligned with neither side could become more important in the runoff. For Flavio Bolsonaro, consolidating support from voters who backed other right-wing and center-right candidates will be important. Lula, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to voters outside his traditional base with measures addressing livelihood concerns, including tighter regulation of online betting and help for indebted households. Turnout will also matter for both sides. With less than 2 percentage points separating the two candidates, mobilizing potential supporters who stayed home could dominate the runoff campaign. HOW COULD U.S. TIES AFFECT THE RACE? Beyond the complex domestic political landscape, the United States has continued to affect this year's election. U.S.-Brazil relations have become increasingly strained over the past year, with disputes ranging from tariffs and judicial proceedings to visa restrictions. The U.S. administration has imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and criticized the conviction of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was found guilty of attempting a coup after losing his reelection bid, while Lula's government has accused Washington of exerting political pressure on Brazil. Those tensions have increasingly intersected with the presidential race. U.S. President Donald Trump, who maintained close ties with Jair Bolsonaro, said shortly before the election that he was watching the Brazilian vote "very closely." Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, has advocated closer ties with Washington, while Lula's campaign has accused the Trump administration of seeking to interfere in Brazil's presidential election. But the U.S. factor may prove counterproductive in electoral terms. Pressure from Washington could give Lula more room to emphasize national sovereignty and resistance to foreign pressure. Daily newspaper Folha de S.Paulo noted that when the United States imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian goods in 2025, Lula's approval ratings rose as his government adopted a stronger sovereignty-focused response. ■

item.title: China Focus: Global businesses eye opportunities as China import expo nears
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
SHANGHAI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- With one month to go before the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE), companies from around the world are preparing to gather in Shanghai in east China, bringing products ranging from advanced manufacturing equipment and medical technologies to African coffee and Syrian soap. The annual expo, the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, has become a major platform for foreign companies seeking access to the vast consumer and industrial markets of the world's second-largest economy. Since its launch in 2018, the CIIE has drawn participants from more than 180 countries, regions and international organizations. Overseas exhibitors have made about 27,000 appearances at its business exhibitions, with over 3,400 new products, technologies and services making their debuts. This year's event, scheduled from Nov. 5 to 10, comes as China begins its 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) with a renewed push for high-standard opening up and stronger domestic demand. For some companies, this year's CIIE will be their first. Austria's WFL Millturn Technologies, a machine tool manufacturer that entered the Chinese market more than 20 years ago, shipped its exhibits from the industrial city of Linz in August. WFL Managing Director Stefan Hackl said the company decided to join the CIIE given China's role at the heart of the global manufacturing chain, and hopes to use the expo to expand further in the Chinese and Asia-Pacific markets. "I don't see any good reason why we will not be successful in China in the upcoming decades," Hackl said. Singapore-based Perennial Holdings Private Limited is another newcomer. The company has established China's first wholly foreign-owned tertiary general hospital in Tianjin in northern China. Since opening, the hospital has received patients from more than 40 countries and regions, while the company is pursuing further healthcare investments in more Chinese cities. "When you invest in China, you are investing in the most competitive market in the world," said Pua Seck Guan, executive chairman and CEO of Perennial Holdings. Pua added that China's opening up of its healthcare sector could create more opportunities for foreign investors. The newcomers arrive as China continues to widen market access for foreign businesses. In 2025, the country registered 70,392 newly established foreign-invested firms, a record high and up 19.1 percent year on year. In the first half of 2026, the number rose 5.3 percent from a year earlier, with foreign direct investment in actual use reaching 402.14 billion yuan (roughly 59.71 billion U.S. dollars). China is also seeking to expand imports as it works to boost domestic consumption and pursue more balanced trade. In August, imports increased by 21.7 percent, with growth exceeding that of exports for a sixth successive month. The opportunities offered by the CIIE extend beyond large multinational companies. Nearly 13,000 overseas micro, small and medium-sized enterprises have participated in the first eight editions. Syrian businessman Muhannad Shakally is preparing for his 9th CIIE. When he brought traditional Syrian soap to the inaugural expo in 2018, he was testing the Chinese market. Today, monthly orders exceed five tonnes, equivalent to around 20,000 bars. "They sell almost as soon as they arrive. I don't even keep inventory," he said. This year, he plans to introduce aromatherapy products and Syrian herbal teas, hoping to bring more products from his country to Chinese consumers. For years, the CIIE has provided free booths to exhibitors from the world's least developed countries. This year, organizers will upgrade a dedicated section for Asian and African products, with measures to help African businesses tap opportunities created by China's zero-tariff policy. Since May 1, China has applied zero-tariff treatment to imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, while expanding market access through measures including upgraded "green channels" for products such as dried chilies, coffee beans, cashews and wild aquatic items. An official delegation from Cote d'Ivoire will make its first appearance at the CIIE's business exhibition, showcasing cocoa, coffee, cashews and kola nuts. "We are very happy to participate for the first time. This will be a good opportunity to showcase Cote d'Ivoire to the world," said Rami Koné, an official with the country's export agency. Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, said small and medium-sized enterprises from the Global South, particularly those in Africa, were once on the margins of global trade. China, he said, has provided them with opportunities to share in the benefits of its opening up and development. ■

item.title: Holiday travel highlights China's transport strength, economic vitality
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Passengers prepare to board a train at Nanjing South Railway Station in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 30, 2026. China's railway network saw a peak in passenger flow on Wednesday, one day before the beginning of the seven-day National Day holiday. (Photo by Su Yang/Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Zhang Yang and his family in Ankang, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, this year's National Day holiday was a memorable one. On Oct. 1, following the opening of the Xi'an-Ankang high-speed railway, they took a direct high-speed train from Ankang to Yan'an, a city known for its revolutionary history. The journey, which used to take more than seven hours, now takes just over two hours. The Zhang family was among millions on the move during the National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, one of China's peak periods for travel and spending. Data from the Ministry of Transport showed cross-regional passenger trips exceeded 300 million on each of the first three days of the holiday. China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said the country's railways handled over 25.2 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record. For a country as vast as China, moving hundreds of millions of people during a holiday rush is a feat of scale. Behind this feat lies a transport network built up over decades. By the end of 2025, China's comprehensive transport network spanned more than 6 million km, including the world's largest high-speed rail network. High-speed railways, expressways, airports and ports connect cities, towns and rural areas across the country. The network is continuing to expand. On Sept. 28, China opened four major high-speed railway sections across northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, with a combined length of more than 1,100 km. The new lines further shorten travel times and put more destinations within easy reach of families like Zhang's. China's transport development goes beyond faster journeys. Better supporting services are also making travel more convenient. New energy vehicles (NEVs) have become increasingly common among Chinese households and are now a popular choice for long-distance travel. The Ministry of Transport expects NEV trips on expressways during the holiday to reach 1.8 times the usual level, pushing up demand for charging services. China's extensive charging infrastructure is helping to meet growing demand. The country now has more than 24 million EV charging facilities, forming the world's largest EV charging network. Highway service areas have about 89,000 charging facilities in total, covering virtually all service areas. To handle the holiday peak, mobile emergency chargers have been added at key service areas, while drivers are encouraged to leave after charging their batteries to 80 percent to improve charging turnover. Faster connections and more convenient services are making it easier for travelers to visit more destinations in a single trip. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that nearly 30 percent of travelers had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year. The trend extends beyond China's borders. China's expanding transport links are supporting a rise in cross-border travel, with Chinese airlines operating regular international passenger routes connecting 177 cities in 80 countries. For outbound travel, Qunar data showed that hotel bookings for multi-country trips more than doubled year on year during the holiday. Inbound tourism also recorded double-digit growth, according to Trip.com Group, with day-tour bookings up more than fourfold and train ticket bookings up more than 170 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks. The transport network that carries millions of travelers is also keeping goods moving, linking businesses and markets and sustaining economic activity across the country. Even during the holiday, the Liujing operating area of Nanning Port in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region bustles with activity, as ship horns sound and workers load and unload goods. The increase in cargo traffic is closely linked to the opening of the Pinglu Canal. Stretching 134.2 km from Hengzhou in Guangxi to the Beibu Gulf, the canal opened to navigation on Sept. 16, providing a shorter river-sea route for cargo from southwest China to international markets. Bulk cargo, including construction materials, auto parts and grain, is being shipped from Nanning Port via the Pinglu Canal to the Beibu Gulf for export. On average, the route now handles an additional 20,000 tonnes of cargo per day. "We expect to transport 200,000 tonnes of cargo during the National Day holiday," said You Tong, deputy manager of the production operations center at Nanning Port Development and Investment Co., Ltd. You said the port has optimized operations and maintained round-the-clock staffing to keep cargo moving smoothly during the holiday surge. ■

item.title: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
* China reaffirmed its continental dominance by topping the gold medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals - its best-ever haul at an overseas Asiad. * The Games signaled a changing of the guard, with 548 of China's 815 athletes making their Asiad debuts and over a quarter born in 2005 or later. * Beyond traditional disciplines, young Chinese athletes broke new ground in skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle-sports aligned with the Olympic program's youth-oriented shift. NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad. Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya. DEPTH ON DISPLAY China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games. Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history. That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records. On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table. The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records. "The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes." Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions. YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later. In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver. Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday. They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence. "Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said. 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images. That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters. "I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said. The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics. The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds. Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media. "These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics." BREAKING NEW GROUND Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports. After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday. "This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium." As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage. China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned. For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal. Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics. "I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time." China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most. 21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut. "I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said. The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport. ■
